questions.question: You are developing an Azure Function in Python by using the v2 programming model. The function must run each time a message arrives in an Azure Service Bus queue named jobs. Which decorator should you use?

options.why: Correct. This trigger starts the function for each message in the jobs queue.
This is an output binding. It writes messages to the queue rather than starting the function.
A timer trigger runs on a schedule and does not react to queue messages.
This defines an HTTP trigger, not a Service Bus trigger.

questions.explanation: In the Python v2 model, triggers and bindings are declared with decorators on a FunctionApp object in function_app.py.

questions.scenario: An HTTP-triggered Python function has the decorator @app.service_bus_queue_output(arg_name="job", queue_name="jobs", connection="ServiceBusConnection") and a parameter named job of type func.Out[str].
questions.question: How should the function send a message to the queue?

options.text: Call job.set() with the message body
options.why: Correct. Setting the value of the output parameter causes the Functions host to send the message.

options.text: Return the message body as the HTTP response
options.why: The HTTP response is returned to the caller. It is not written to the queue binding.

options.text: Create a ServiceBusClient inside the function and call send_messages
options.why: This works but bypasses the output binding that is already declared, which is the purpose of the requirement.

options.text: Call job.get() with the message body
options.why: func.Out exposes set() for output values. get() is not used to send output.

questions.explanation: Output bindings in Python use func.Out[T]. The value passed to set() is written to the target service when the function completes.

questions.question: A Python function is triggered by an Azure Service Bus queue and uses the default trigger settings. The function raises an unhandled exception for a message. What happens to the message?

options.text: The message is abandoned and delivered again until the maximum delivery count is reached, after which it is moved to the dead-letter queue
options.why: Correct. The trigger completes messages on success and abandons them on failure.
The trigger uses peek-lock, so a failure does not delete the message.

options.text: The message is deferred and can be retrieved only by sequence number
options.why: The trigger does not defer messages automatically.

options.text: The message is retried indefinitely every second
options.why: Retries are limited by the maximum delivery count of the queue.

questions.explanation: Service Bus retries the message through redelivery. Design the function to be idempotent because a message can be processed more than once.

questions.question: An HTTP-triggered function must be callable only by clients that supply a key specific to that function. The function must not require the host master key. Which authorization level should you set?

options.why: Correct. Callers must supply a function key or host key in the x-functions-key header or code query string.
Anonymous functions require no key, so any caller can invoke them.
Admin level requires the master key, which the requirement excludes.
SYSTEM is not an HTTP authorization level for function code.

questions.explanation: The authorization levels for HTTP triggers are ANONYMOUS, FUNCTION, and ADMIN. FUNCTION is the default.

questions.question: A function must rebuild a search index at 02:00 every day. Which trigger configuration should you use?

options.why: Correct. The six-field NCRONTAB expression runs at second 0, minute 0, hour 2 every day.
This is a five-field cron expression. The timer trigger expects six fields that start with seconds.
An Event Grid trigger reacts to events, not to a schedule.
An HTTP trigger needs an external caller and does not run on a schedule by itself.

questions.explanation: The timer trigger uses NCRONTAB expressions in the format {second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}.
